claim: H3K9 methylation (H3K9me) specifies the establishment and maintenance of transcriptionally silent epigenetic states or heterochromatin.
source: H3K9 methylation (H3K9me) specifies the establishment and maintenance of transcriptionally silent epigenetic states or heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of epigenetics.

claim: Epe1 is a putative histone demethylase in fission yeast that has a non-enzymatic function opposing heterochromatin assembly.
source: Here, we reveal an inversion of this paradigm where a putative histone demethylase Epe1 in fission yeast, has a non-enzymatic function that opposes heterochromatin assembly.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental approaches throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutations within the putative catalytic JmjC domain of Epe1 disrupt its interaction with Swi6HP1.
source: Mutations within the putative catalytic JmjC domain of Epe1 disrupt its interaction with Swi6HP1 suggesting that this domain might have other functions besides enzymatic activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and in vitro binding assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: The C-terminus of Epe1 directly interacts with Swi6HP1.
source: The C-terminus of Epe1 directly interacts with Swi6HP1, and H3K9 methylation stimulates this protein-protein interaction in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding assays and co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: H3K9 methylation stimulates the protein-protein interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 in vitro and in vivo.
source: The C-terminus of Epe1 directly interacts with Swi6HP1, and H3K9 methylation stimulates this protein-protein interaction in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding assays with H3K9me3 peptides (Figure 4) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments in clr4Δ and H3K9R mutant cells.

claim: Expressing the Epe1 C-terminus is sufficient to disrupt heterochromatin by outcompeting the histone deacetylase Clr3 from sites of heterochromatin formation.
source: Expressing the Epe1 C-terminus is sufficient to disrupt heterochromatin by outcompeting the histone deacetylase, Clr3 from sites of heterochromatin formation.
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene assays (Figure 3E) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing altered Clr3-Swi6HP1 interactions (Figure 6A).

claim: Heterochromatin formation is critical for centromere and telomere function, silencing of transposons and repetitive DNA elements, and for maintaining lineage-specific patterns of gene expression.
source: Heterochromatin formation is critical for centromere and telomere function, silencing of transposons and repetitive DNA elements, and for maintaining lineage-specific patterns of gene expression (Grewal and Jia, 2007; Nicetto et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The establishment of H3K9 methylation requires the enzymatic activity of a conserved methyltransferase, Clr4Suv39h.
source: In fission yeast, the establishment of H3K9 methylation requires the enzymatic activity of a conserved methyltransferase, Clr4Suv39h (Rea et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Two HP1 homologs, Swi6HP1 and Chp2HP1, are involved in H3K9 methylation binding and have distinct, non-overlapping functions during transcriptional silencing.
source: Two HP1 homologs, Swi6HP1 and Chp2HP1, are involved in H3K9 methylation binding and have distinct, non-overlapping functions during transcriptional silencing (Motamedi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Epe1, a putative histone demethylase, promotes epigenetic erasure, thus reversing H3K9 methylation and transcriptional gene silencing.
source: Ultimately, factors such as Epe1, a putative histone demethylase, promote epigenetic erasure, thus reversing H3K9 methylation and transcriptional gene silencing (Ayoub et al., 2003; Trewick et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: H3K9 methylation spreads to silence genes that are distant from heterochromatin nucleation centers.
source: Once established, H3K9 methylation spreads to silence genes that are distant from heterochromatin nucleation centers.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: H3K9me spreading depends on the read-write activity of Clr4Suv39h.
source: H3K9me spreading depends on the read-write activity of Clr4Suv39h (Al-Sady et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Clr4Suv39h has a conserved chromodomain that recognizes and binds to H3K9me and an enzymatic SET domain that is involved in catalysis.
source: Two conserved, structural attributes of Clr4Suv39h mediate this process: a conserved chromodomain that recognizes and binds to H3K9me and an enzymatic SET domain that is involved in catalysis (Ivanova et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The ability of Clr4Suv39h to bind to the product of its enzymatic activity enables H3K9 methylated histones to serve as carriers of epigenetic information.
source: The ability of Clr4Suv39h to bind to the product of its enzymatic activity enables H3K9 methylated histones to serve as carriers of epigenetic information (Audergon et al., 2015; Ragunathan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: H3K9 methylation acts as a multivalent platform that recruits the HP1 homolog, Swi6HP1 to sites of constitutive heterochromatin.
source: H3K9 methylation acts as a multivalent platform that recruits the HP1 homolog, Swi6HP1 to sites of constitutive heterochromatin (Ekwall et al., 1995; Ekwall et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HP1 proteins have a conserved architecture consisting of a chromodomain (CD) that is involved in H3K9 methylation binding and a dimerization domain called the chromoshadow domain (CSD) that mediates protein-protein interactions.
source: HP1 proteins have a conserved architecture consisting of a chromodomain (CD) that is involved in H3K9 methylation binding and a dimerization domain called the chromoshadow domain (CSD) that mediates protein-protein interactions (Bannister et al., 2001; Cowieson et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The oligomerization of HP1 proteins promotes formation of higher-order chromatin complexes that exhibit phase separated, liquid-like properties in vitro and in cells.
source: The oligomerization of HP1 proteins promotes formation of higher-order chromatin complexes that exhibit phase separated, liquid-like properties in vitro and in cells (Larson et al., 2017; Sanulli et al., 2018; Strom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Recruitment of Epe1, a putative histone demethylase that opposes heterochromatin formation, is dependent on Swi6HP1.
source: Most notably, recruitment of Epe1, a putative histone demethylase that opposes heterochromatin formation, is dependent on Swi6HP1 (Ayoub et al., 2003; Zofall and Grewal, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of Epe1 leads to increased heterochromatin spreading beyond normal boundary sequences.
source: Loss of Epe1 leads to increased heterochromatin spreading beyond normal boundary sequences, inheritance of H3K9 methylation via sequence-independent pathways, increased cell to cell variation in H3K9 methylation patterns, and acquisition of adaptive epigenetic traits (Audergon et al., 2015; Ayoub et al., 2003; Ragunathan et al., 2015; Sorida et al., 2019; Trewick et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2015; Zofall and Grewal, 2006; Zofall et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Epe1 most closely resembles JumonjiC (JmjC) domain containing proteins that use Fe (II) and α-ketoglutarate as co-factors to catalyze histone demethylation.
source: Epe1 most closely resembles JumonjiC (JmjC) domain containing proteins that use Fe (II) and α-ketoglutarate as co-factors to catalyze histone demethylation (Tsukada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Unlike active histone demethylases, where an HxD/E….H motif is involved in Fe (II) coordination, Epe1 harbors a non-canonical HXE….Y motif.
source: Unlike active histone demethylases, where an HxD/E….H motif is involved in Fe (II) coordination, Epe1 harbors a non-canonical HXE….Y motif (Tsukada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Epe1 purified from fission yeast cells, or a recombinant source (insect cells), exhibits no H3K9 demethylase activity in vitro.
source: Epe1 purified from fission yeast cells, or a recombinant source (insect cells), exhibits no H3K9 demethylase activity in vitro (Tsukada et al., 2006; Zofall and Grewal, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and demethylase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Point mutations of amino acid residues involved in Fe (II) or α-ketoglutarate binding affect Epe1 activity in cells and lead to heterochromatin spreading beyond normal boundary sequences.
source: However, point mutations of amino acid residues involved in Fe (II) or α-ketoglutarate binding affect Epe1 activity in cells and lead to heterochromatin spreading beyond normal boundary sequences (Trewick et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: The overexpression of Fe (II) and α-ketoglutarate binding mutants of Epe1 suppresses heterochromatin spreading defects observed in epe1Δ strains.
source: In support of this hypothesis, the overexpression of Fe (II) and α-ketoglutarate binding mutants of Epe1 suppresses heterochromatin spreading defects observed in epe1Δ strains (Trewick et al., 2007; Zofall and Grewal, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The putative catalytic JmjC domain of Epe1 is, at least in part, dispensable for its anti-silencing function in cells.
source: In this study, we discovered that the putative catalytic JmjC domain of Epe1 is, at least in part, dispensable for its anti-silencing function in cells.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that the Epe1 C-terminus (Epe1434-948) lacking the JmjC domain can partially restore anti-silencing activity (Figure 3C-D).

claim: A cis interaction between the Epe1 N- and C-terminus inhibits Swi6HP1 binding.
source: We propose that a cis interaction between the Epe1 N- and C-terminus inhibits Swi6HP1 binding.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding assays showing that the N- and C-terminal fragments of Epe1 interact in trans (Figure 3B) and that the C-terminal fragment alone shows enhanced Swi6HP1 binding (Figure 3A).

claim: H3K9 methylation binding attenuates the intramolecular interaction between Epe1 N- and C-terminus and promotes Swi6HP1 binding.
source: H3K9 methylation binding attenuates this intramolecular interaction and promotes Swi6HP1 binding.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding assays showing that H3K9me3 peptides disrupt the trans interaction between Epe1-N and Epe1-C (Figure 5C) and stimulate Epe1-Swi6HP1 interaction (Figure 4C-D).

claim: Alanine substitutions of amino acid residues involved in Fe (II) or α-ketoglutarate binding (epe1 H297A and epe1 Y307A, respectively) disrupt co-factor binding, resulting in the concomitant loss of Epe1 activity.
source: Alanine substitutions of amino acid residues involved in Fe (II) or α-ketoglutarate binding (epe1 H297A and epe1 Y307A, respectively) disrupt co-factor binding, resulting in the concomitant loss of Epe1 activity.
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene assays showing red or sectored colonies in these mutants (Figure 1B).

claim: Replacing the non-conserved tyrosine residue in Epe1 with alanine (epe1 Y370A) leads to a similar loss of function phenotype.
source: Replacing the non-conserved tyrosine residue in Epe1 with alanine (epe1 Y370A) leads to a similar loss of function phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene assays showing red or sectored colonies in this mutant (Figure 1B).

claim: Both wild-type and Epe1 mutant strains exhibit high levels of H3K9me2 during establishment.
source: Both wild-type and Epe1 mutant strains exhibit high levels of H3K9me2 during establishment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 1C.

claim: Wild-type cells lose H3K9me2 approximately 24 h after tetracycline addition.
source: However, wild-type cells lose H3K9me2 approximately 24 h after tetracycline addition.
evidence: This is shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 1D.

claim: Epe1 mutants that exhibit a red or sectored phenotype upon +tetracycline addition retain high levels of H3K9 methylation at the ectopic site.
source: In contrast, Epe1 mutants that exhibit a red or sectored phenotype upon +tetracycline addition retain high levels of H3K9 methylation at the ectopic site (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 1D.

claim: Epe1 is localized at sites of constitutive heterochromatin through its interactions with Swi6HP1.
source: Epe1 is localized at sites of constitutive heterochromatin through its interactions with Swi6HP1 (Ayoub et al., 2003; Zofall and Grewal, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: mNeonGreen-Epe1 co-localizes with mCherry-Swi6HP1 at sites of constitutive heterochromatin.
source: mNeonGreen-Epe1 co-localizes with mCherry-Swi6HP1 as evidenced by the significant overlap between the bright foci that appear green and red emission channels (see white arrows).
evidence: This is directly shown in the live cell imaging data in Figure 1E.

claim: An Epe1 co-factor binding mutant, mNeonGreen-Epe1 Y307A, fails to co-localize with mCherry-Swi6HP1.
source: Surprisingly, an Epe1 co-factor binding mutant, mNeonGreen-Epe1 Y307A, fails to co-localize with mCherry-Swi6HP1. Instead, the mutant protein exhibits a diffuse green signal within the nucleus and a complete lack of nuclear foci that co-localize with Swi6HP1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is directly shown in the live cell imaging data in Figure 1F.

claim: Swi6HP1 is enriched in pull-down experiments in wild-type cells relative to an untagged control.
source: Swi6HP1 is enriched in pull-down experiments in wild-type cells relative to an untagged control (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2A.

claim: Mutations in residues that affect Fe(II) or α-ketoglutarate binding (H297A, Y307A, and Y370A) significantly attenuate the interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1.
source: However, mutations in residues that affect Fe(II) or α-ketoglutarate binding (H297A, Y307A, and Y370A) significantly attenuate this interaction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2A.

claim: Epe1 is enriched within dg repeats in wild-type cells and this heterochromatin-specific occupancy pattern is disrupted both in swi6Δ and clr4Δ cells.
source: Epe1 is enriched within dg repeats in wild-type cells and this heterochromatin-specific occupancy pattern is disrupted both in swi6Δ and clr4Δ cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: Mutations within the JmjC domain that disrupt co-factor binding lead to a substantial reduction in Epe1 occupancy at sites of heterochromatin formation.
source: Mutations within the JmjC domain that disrupt co-factor binding lead to a substantial reduction in Epe1 occupancy at sites of heterochromatin formation.
evidence: This is shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: Wild-type Epe1 and Epe1 H297A exhibit similar denaturation temperatures, implying that the mutation within the JmjC domain does not destabilize the protein or cause substantial alterations in protein structure.
source: Wild-type Epe1 and Epe1 H297A exhibit similar denaturation temperatures, implying that the mutation within the JmjC domain does not destabilize the protein or cause substantial alterations in protein structure.
evidence: This is shown in the differential scanning calorimetry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Epe1 preferentially interacts with Swi6HP1 as opposed to a second HP1 homolog in S. pombe, Chp2HP1.
source: We verified that the Epe1 protein we purified from insect cells preferentially interacts with Swi6HP1 as opposed to a second HP1 homolog in S. pombe, Chp2HP1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 2C.

claim: A dimerization deficient mutant of Swi6 (Swi6HP1 L315E) exhibits a significant reduction in its ability to interact with Epe1.
source: Our binding assays using the mutant Swi6HP1 protein (Swi6HP1 L315E) reveal a significant reduction in its ability to interact with Epe1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 2D.

claim: The Fe (II) binding deficient mutant, Epe1 H297A, shows reduced binding to Swi6HP1 compared to wild-type Epe1.
source: Adding increasing quantities of the wild-type MBP-Epe1 leads to a corresponding increase in the amount of protein that interacts with Swi6HP1. However, this type of interaction and increase in binding is not observed in the case of MBP-Epe1 H297A (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 2E.

claim: The interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 is nearly identical in the presence or absence of EDTA.
source: The interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 is nearly identical in the presence or absence of EDTA (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 2E.

claim: The addition of co-factors required for histone demethylation did not alter the extent of interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1.
source: The addition of co-factors required for histone demethylation did not alter the extent of interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Swi6HP1 binding to Epe1 is not sufficient to activate its putative enzymatic functions.
source: Hence, Swi6HP1 binding to Epe1 is not sufficient to activate its putative enzymatic functions.
evidence: This is supported by demethylase assay data showing no mass shift corresponding to demethylation in reactions with Epe1 alone or Epe1 in complex with Swi6HP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: A C-terminal fragment of Epe1 spanning 434–948 amino acids and an N-terminal fragment of Epe1 encompassing 1–600 amino acids (Epe1-ΔC) emerged as putative Swi6HP1 interaction candidates.
source: A C-terminal fragment of Epe1 spanning 434–948 amino acids and an N-terminal fragment of Epe1 encompassing 1–600 amino acids (Epe1-ΔC) emerged as putative Swi6HP1 interaction candidates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro translation assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Epe1 C-terminal fragment exhibits an increase in its interaction with Swi6HP1 relative to full-length Epe1.
source: The Epe1 C-terminal fragment exhibits an increase in its interaction with Swi6HP1 relative to full-length Epe1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 3A.

claim: The addition of recombinant Swi6HP1 is sufficient to compete with and disrupt a trans interaction between the Epe1-N and Epe1-C fragments.
source: The addition of recombinant Swi6HP1 is sufficient to compete with and disrupt a trans interaction between the Epe1-N and Epe1-C fragments (Figure 3B, lane 2).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 3B.

claim: Expressing Epe1434-948 protein results in a phenotype that is substantially different compared to Epe1 co-factor binding mutants or epe1Δ cells.
source: The expression of the Epe1 C-terminal fragment, Epe1434-948 results in a phenotype that is substantially different compared to Epe1 co-factor binding mutants or epe1Δ cells.
evidence: This is shown in the reporter gene assay data in Figure 3C.

claim: There is a three-fold reduction in the number of red or sectored colonies in the Epe1 JmjCΔ mutant compared to Epe1 null cells.
source: We observed a three-fold reduction in the number of red or sectored colonies in the Epe1 JmjCΔ mutant compared to Epe1 null cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly shown in the quantification data in Figure 3D.

claim: The C-terminal fragment of Epe1 (Epe1434-948), which is devoid of the JmjC domain, completely blocks heterochromatin establishment in the TetR-Swi6-CSD system.
source: Remarkably, this C-terminal fragment, which is devoid of the JmjC domain, completely blocks heterochromatin establishment. Cells remain white in the presence or absence of +tetracycline (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is directly shown in the reporter gene assay data in Figure 3E.

claim: The interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 is obliterated in both H3K9 methylation deficient mutant strains, clr4Δ and H3K9R mutants.
source: Although Epe1 interacts with Swi6HP1 in wild-type cells, this interaction is obliterated in both of the H3K9 methylation deficient mutant strains, clr4Δ and H3K9R mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A.

claim: Deleting histone deacetylases Sir2 or Clr3, both of which affect heterochromatin formation and Swi6HP1 localization, resulted in a substantial decrease in the interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1.
source: Furthermore, deleting histone deacetylases Sir2 or Clr3, both of which affect heterochromatin formation and Swi6HP1 localization, also resulted in a substantial decrease in the interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4B.

claim: Epe1 exhibits a significant increase in its ability to interact with Swi6HP1 in the presence of an H3K9me3 peptide.
source: Compared to reactions where no-peptide (lanes 1–3) or an unmethylated H3 peptide was added (lanes 4–6), we observed a substantial increase in the interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 specifically in the presence of an H3K9me3 peptide (lanes 7–9) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: An H3K9me2 peptide was also capable of stimulating the interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 compared to reactions where no peptide was added or assays where an unmodified peptide was used.
source: An H3K9me2 peptide was also capable of stimulating the interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 compared to reactions where no peptide was added or assays where an unmodified peptide was used (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The addition of an H3K4me3 peptide fails to enhance complex formation between Epe1 and Swi6HP1.
source: The addition of an H3K4me3 peptide fails to enhance complex formation between Epe1 and Swi6HP1, unlike the significant enhancement in binding we observed upon addition of an H3K9me3 peptide (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 4D.

claim: Despite Swi6HP1 W104A being unable to bind to an H3K9me3 tail peptide, a stimulation in the interaction between Epe1 and the Swi6HP1 (W104A) was observed in the presence of an H3K9me3 peptide.
source: Despite Swi6HP1 being unable to bind to an H3K9me3 tail peptide, we observed a stimulation in the interaction between Epe1 and the Swi6HP1 (W104A) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 4E.

claim: Epe1 remains responsive to the presence of an H3K9 methylated peptide even in a context where Swi6HP1 is constitutively released from auto-inhibition (Loop-X mutant).
source: Therefore, Epe1 remains responsive to the presence of an H3K9 methylated peptide even in a context where Swi6HP1 is constitutively released from auto-inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Epe1 directly binds to an H3K9me3 peptide as opposed to an unmodified H3K9me0 peptide.
source: Our binding assays detect a direct interaction between Epe1 and an H3K9me3 peptide as opposed to an unmodified H3K9me0 peptide.
evidence: This is shown in the peptide binding assay data in Figure 5A.

claim: Epe1 selectively interacts with H3K9 methylated histones as opposed to H3K4 methylated histones.
source: Furthermore, Epe1 selectively interacts with H3K9 methylated histones as opposed to H3K4 methylated histones. (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the histone binding assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: Epe1-ΔC can also directly bind to an H3K9me3 peptide and specifically interacts with H3K9 methylated histones.
source: We found that Epe1-ΔC can also directly bind to an H3K9me3 peptide and specifically interacts with H3K9 methylated histones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the binding assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The H3K9me3 peptide specifically disrupts a direct trans interaction between the N- and C-terminal halves of Epe1.
source: We observed an interaction in trans between the N- and C-terminal halves of Epe1 in binding assays with no peptide or an H3K9me0 peptide. However, the addition of an H3K9me3 peptide eliminates the interaction between the N- and C-terminal fragments of Epe1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: A substantial increase in the interaction between Epe1-ΔC and Swi6HP1 was detected compared to a weak interaction in the case of the full-length protein.
source: Our co-IP assays detect a substantial increase in the interaction between Epe1-ΔC and Swi6HP1, compared to a weak interaction in the case of the full-length protein and no interaction in the case of Epe1-N (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Epe1-ΔC significantly outperforms the full-length protein in its ability to interact with Swi6HP1.
source: Epe1-ΔC significantly outperforms the full-length protein in its ability to interact with Swi6HP1 (compare lanes 4–6 with lanes 1–3) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 5D.

claim: The addition of a modified peptide had no effect on the interaction between Swi6HP1 and Epe1-ΔC.
source: Surprisingly, the addition of a modified peptide had no effect on the interaction between Swi6HP1 and Epe1-ΔC (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is directly shown in the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 5E.

claim: Unlike the full-length Epe1 protein, an interaction between Epe1-ΔC and Swi6HP1 was observed in both clr4+ and clr4Δ cells.
source: Consistent with our in vitro binding assays and unlike the full-length Epe1 protein, we observed an interaction between Epe1-ΔC and Swi6HP1 in both clr4+ and clr4Δ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The interaction between Swi6HP1 and Clr3 substantially increases in an Epe1 H297A strain background compared to wild-type Epe1.
source: We measured a weak interaction between Swi6HP1 and Clr3 in a wild-type Epe1 background that substantially increases in an Epe1 H297A strain background (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6A.

claim: The increase in interaction between Clr3 and Swi6HP1 occurs in the absence of any increase in Swi6HP1 occupancy at the pericentromeric repeats.
source: This positive change in the interaction between Clr3 and Swi6HP1 occurs in the absence of any increase in Swi6HP1 occupancy at the pericentromeric repeats (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 6B.

claim: Epe1 enrichment is increased two to three-fold at dg pericentromeric repeats in clr3Δ strains.
source: Consistent with our model, we observed a three-fold increase in Epe1 localization at the pericentromeric dg repeats and the mating type locus (mat) (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is directly shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 6C.

claim: The deletion of clr3Δ results in the complete loss of Epe1 localization at the telomeres.
source: In contrast, the deletionof clr3Δ results in the complete loss of Epe1 localization at the telomeres (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is directly shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 6E.

claim: The constitutive tethering of Clr3 but not Sir2 promotes epigenetic inheritance.
source: However, upon exposure to tetracycline, the constitutive tethering of Clr3 but not Sir2 promotes epigenetic inheritance. Cells exhibit a red and sectored phenotype in cells where Clr3 is artificially tethered, despite Epe1 still being present (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the reporter gene assay data in Figure 7B.

claim: Cells maintain high H3K9me2 levels in the presence of Gal4-Clr3 before and after tetracycline.
source: We measured changes in H3K9me2 levels associated with the ade6+ reporter gene using ChIP-qPCR. Cells maintain high H3K9me2 levels in the presence of Gal4-Clr3 before and after tetracycline (Figure 7C-D).
evidence: This is directly shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Gal4-Clr3 cannot initiate H3K9 methylation de novo in fission yeast.
source: Hence, Gal4-Clr3 cannot initiate H3K9 methylation de novo in fission yeast (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is shown in the reporter gene assay and ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Clr3 must be recruited in cis to oppose the anti-silencing effects of Epe1.
source: Therefore, Clr3 must be recruited in cis to oppose the anti-silencing effects of Epe1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the reporter gene assay data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells that are initially red in –tetracycline medium turn white on +tetracycline medium in a clr4ΔCD expressing mutant.
source: Cells that are initially red in –tetracycline medium turn white on +tetracycline medium in a clr4ΔCD expressing mutant (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is directly shown in the reporter gene assay data in Figure 7E.

claim: The inheritance of H3K9 methylation depends on the read-write activity of Clr4Suv39h despite Clr3 being constitutively tethered.
source: Hence, the inheritance of H3K9 methylation depends on the read-write activity of Clr4Suv39h despite Clr3 being constitutively tethered (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: This is shown in the ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 7F, G.

claim: The enzymatic erasure of histone modifications is widely assumed to be the primary mechanism that reverses epigenetic silencing.
source: The enzymatic erasure of histone modifications is widely assumed to be the primary mechanism that reverses epigenetic silencing.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Passive genome-wide nucleosome exchange can compete with histone modification-dependent read-write mechanisms to oppose epigenetic inheritance.
source: In principle, passive genome-wide nucleosome exchange can compete with histone modification-dependent read-write mechanisms to oppose epigenetic inheritance.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the discussion of histone turnover and its effects on epigenetic inheritance.

claim: Enzymatic erasure is at least in part, dispensable for regulating the inheritance of transcriptionally silent epigenetic states in fission yeast.
source: Our data support the notion that enzymatic erasure is at least in part, dispensable for regulating the inheritance of transcriptionally silent epigenetic states in fission yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Epe1 has newly defined roles in recruiting members of the SAGA complex which mediate histone acetylation, a chromatin feature that is also associated with increased nucleosome turnover.
source: In addition, Epe1 also has newly defined roles in recruiting members of the SAGA complex which mediate histone acetylation, a chromatin feature that is also associated with increased nucleosome turnover (Bao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: The N-terminus of Epe1 has a function in transcriptional activation, which suppresses stochastic, epigenetic silencing.
source: Recent work demonstrated a surprising and unexpected function for the N-terminus of Epe1 in transcriptional activation, which suppresses stochastic, epigenetic silencing (Sorida et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Auto-inhibition is a widely used strategy that proteins use to activate their latent functions in response to specific cellular or environmental signals.
source: Auto-inhibition is a widely used strategy that proteins use to activate their latent functions in response to specific cellular or environmental signals (Pufall and Graves, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Swi6HP1 is auto-inhibited by a histone H3 mimic sequence.
source: The non-catalytic heterochromatin associated protein Swi6HP1 is auto-inhibited by a histone H3 mimic sequence (Canzio et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Swi6HP1 is dynamic and undergoes rapid exchange on the millisecond timescale between the free and H3K9 methylation-bound state.
source: Swi6HP1 is dynamic and undergoes rapid exchange on the millisecond timescale between the free and H3K9 methylation-bound state (Cheutin et al., 2004; Cheutin et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: By enforcing an H3K9 methylation-dependent mode of interaction, Epe1 selectively targets a sub-population of Swi6HP1 molecules that are bound to sites of H3K9 methylation and have a causal role in heterochromatin formation.
source: By enforcing an H3K9 methylation-dependent mode of interaction, Epe1 selectively targets a sub-population of Swi6HP1 molecules that are bound to sites of H3K9 methylation and have a causal role in heterochromatin formation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the experimental data showing H3K9 methylation-dependent interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1.

claim: Swi6HP1 phosphorylation compromises Epe1 binding and promotes histone deacetylase recruitment to sites of heterochromatin formation.
source: For example, Swi6HP1 phosphorylation compromises Epe1 binding and promotes histone deacetylase recruitment to sites of heterochromatin formation (Shimada et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Tethering Clr3 at an ectopic site renders heterochromatin refractory to the anti-silencing effects of Epe1.
source: Tethering Clr3 at an ectopic site renders heterochromatin refractory to the anti-silencing effects of Epe1.
evidence: This is supported by the reporter gene assay data in Figure 7B.

claim: DNA binding proteins, Atf1 and Pcr1 recruit Clr3 to maintain epigenetic silencing following an RNAi-dependent initiation mechanism at the fission yeast mating type locus.
source: Our observations are in part, similar to previous findings relating to the fission yeast mating type locus where DNA binding proteins, Atf1 and Pcr1 recruit Clr3 to maintain epigenetic silencing following an RNAi-dependent initiation mechanism (Wang and Moazed, 2017; Yamada et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Histone deacetylases such as Clr3 create a chromatin environment that promotes the read-write enzymatic function of Clr4Suv39h.
source: We favor a model where histone deacetylases such as Clr3 create a chromatin environment that promotes the read-write enzymatic function of Clr4Suv39h.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data showing that Clr3 tethering promotes H3K9 methylation maintenance.

claim: Epe1 prevents Clr3 mediated histone hypoacetylation by forming an inhibitory complex with Swi6HP1 within a heterochromatin restricted genomic context.
source: In essence, Epe1 prevents Clr3 mediated histone hypoacetylation by forming an inhibitory complex with Swi6HP1 within a heterochromatin restricted genomic context.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that Epe1 displaces Clr3 from Swi6HP1.

claim: A histone demethylase like protein in Neurospora, DMM-1 shares many similarities with Epe1 and also surprisingly lacks any in vitro enzymatic activity.
source: It is noteworthy that a histone demethylase like protein in Neurospora, DMM-1 shares many similarities with Epe1 and also surprisingly lacks any in vitro enzymatic activity (Honda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: DMM-1 also interacts with the HP1 homolog in Neurospora.
source: DMM-1 also interacts with the HP1 homolog in Neurospora leading us to speculate that this surprising mode of heterochromatin regulation we uncovered in the case of Epe1 might also extend to other fungal systems.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and represents a speculative inference.

claim: Expressing the C-terminus of Epe1 only partially restores wild-type levels of Epe1 activity.
source: Given that expressing the C-terminus of Epe1 only partially restores wild-type levels of Epe1 activity (Figure 3C,D), we speculate that there could potentially be unique substrates or conditions required to reconstitute the enzymatic activity of Epe1.
evidence: This is shown in the reporter gene assay data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Bdf2, a BRD4 homolog that localizes to heterochromatin boundaries along with Epe1, is a possible candidate that may activate the latent enzymatic functions of Epe1.
source: For example, Bdf2, a BRD4 homolog that localizes to heterochromatin boundaries along with Epe1, is a possible candidate that may activate the latent enzymatic functions of Epe1 as H3K9 methylation levels are negligible at the heterochromatin-euchromatin boundary (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the localization of Bdf2 and Epe1, supported by a citation.

claim: The Drosophila protein dKDM4A is a prominent example of a histone demethylase with enzymatic and non-enzymatic functions.
source: The Drosophila protein dKDM4A is a prominent example of a histone demethylase with enzymatic and non-enzymatic functions (Colmenares et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: JARID2, a subunit of the PRC2 complex, shares several characteristics with JmjC domain-containing proteins but has a structural role in regulating PRC2 complex assembly.
source: More extreme examples of histone-modifying enzyme mimicry are observed in the case of JARID2, a subunit of the PRC2 complex that shares several characteristics with JmjC domain-containing proteins but has a structural role in regulating PRC2 complex assembly (Kasinath et al., 2018; Son et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Proteins involved in the Arabidopsis RNA-dependent DNA methylation pathway, SUVH2 and SUVH9, resemble SET domain methyltransferases but lack enzymatic activity.
source: Proteins involved in the Arabidopsis RNA-dependent DNA methylation pathway, SUVH2 and SUVH9, resemble SET domain methyltransferases but lack enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SUVH2 and SUVH9 recognize methylated DNA and are involved in RNA pol V recruitment in plants to establish epigenetic silencing.
source: Instead, both proteins recognize methylated DNA and are involved in RNA pol V recruitment in plants to establish epigenetic silencing (Johnson et al., 2008; Law et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It is possible that the putative catalytic function of Epe1 has been repurposed to regulate its interaction with Swi6HP1.
source: Although Epe1 has a JmjC domain, it is possible that its putative catalytic function has been repurposed to regulate its interaction with Swi6HP1.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data showing that JmjC domain mutations affect Swi6HP1 binding.

claim: H3K9 methylation promotes the cooperative assembly of complexes between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 at sites of heterochromatin formation.
source: Our data suggest that H3K9 methylation promotes the cooperative assembly of complexes between Epe1 and Swi6HP1 at sites of heterochromatin formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing H3K9 methylation-dependent interaction between Epe1 and Swi6HP1.

claim: The enzymatic and non-enzymatic functions of Epe1 are likely to oppose heterochromatin assembly on different timescales.
source: We speculate that the enzymatic and non-enzymatic functions of Epe1 are likely to oppose heterochromatin assembly on different timescales.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The non-enzymatic function of Epe1 serves as the first line of opposition to heterochromatin establishment.
source: Hence, the non-enzymatic function of Epe1 serves as the first line of opposition to heterochromatin establishment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that the Epe1 C-terminus can disrupt heterochromatin.

claim: The transient inhibition of heterochromatin assembly by Epe1 is likely to be followed by a slower enzymatic step where Epe1 might demethylate H3K9 methylated histones or activate transcription.
source: This transient inhibition of heterochromatin assembly is likely to be followed by a slower enzymatic step where Epe1 might demethylate H3K9 methylated histones or activate transcription (Sorida et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data and supported by a citation.
